# QR Symbology Architecture

Design record for supporting multiple QR symbologies, Standard QR (ISO/IEC 18004), Micro QR (ISO/IEC 18004), and rMQR (ISO/IEC 23941), in one library. This document defines how the codebase is organized so each symbology can be added without destabilizing the others. Implementation details live in code comments next to the code.

---

## What

### Symbology status

| Symbology | Standard | Encode | Matrix decode | Image decode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard QR (versions 1–40) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2) |
| Micro QR (M1–M4) | ISO/IEC 18004 | Shipped | Shipped | Shipped (Tier 1–2, conservative measured envelope) |
| rMQR (R7x43–R17x139) | ISO/IEC 23941 | Encode + render done (Phase 5, encoder MVT met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 6, decoder MVT matrix rows met; not yet released) | Done (Phase 7, Tier 1–2, measured envelope incl. keystone up to 4 % on R17x139; not yet released) |

### Document set

Specs are one set of files per symbology plus this cross-cutting record, see the [documentation index](../README.md) for the file list. Structure and naming rules live in [docs_authoring_guidelines.md](../docs_authoring_guidelines.md); new symbologies copy the section skeleton of the Standard QR document of the same type.

### Internal organization

Internals are split into shared primitives and per-symbology pipelines.

**Shared primitives** (`Internals`, `Internals.BinaryEncoders`, `Internals.BinaryDecoders`, `Internals.ImageDecoders`), knowledge that is identical across all three symbologies:

| Component | Why it is shared |
|---|---|
| `GaloisField`, `Polynom`, `EccBinaryEncoder`, `EccBinaryDecoder` | All three symbologies use Reed-Solomon over GF(256) with the same primitive polynomial (0x11D) |
| `BitWriter`, `BitReader` | Bit-stream packing is symbology-independent |
| `ModuleBitPacker` | Byte-per-module ↔ MSB-first bit-packed conversion of the Micro QR and rMQR data models (`SetCoreData` / `GetCoreData`) is the same operation for both; Standard QR's `QRCodeData` keeps its own (frozen) storage kernel |
| `ECCInfo` | RS block structure (data codewords, ECC per block, up to two block groups) describes all three symbologies |
| `BinaryInterleaver` | Block interleaving of data then ECC codewords depends only on the `ECCInfo` block structure; Standard QR and rMQR interleave identically (Micro QR has one block). Lifted from `Internals.StandardQR` to `Internals.BinaryEncoders` when rMQR became the second consumer (rMQR Phase 5.4); the only symbology-specific input, the remainder-bit count, is passed in by the caller |
| `EccBlockDecoder` | The matrix decoders' Reed-Solomon block stage: the stream deinterleaved into its blocks, the exact inverse of `BinaryInterleaver`, each block corrected up to a capacity the symbology passes, and the data gathered in block order. Standard QR and rMQR run it; Micro QR has one block and a half codeword, and corrects it itself. Until 2026-09-29 Standard QR and rMQR each wrote the stage out, rMQR as its own fused loop; sharing it changed no read and no status, and rMQR's loop put back measured 1.6 to 2.8 % slower than the shared stage on a matrix with errors. A single block is its own interleaving and is corrected in place, without the deinterleave and the copy back (2026-10-01): 29 of rMQR's 64 versions and levels have one, and 12 of Standard QR's 160, all at versions 1 to 5 |
| `EncodingMode`, `TextAnalyzer`, `CharacterSets` | Mode alphabet definitions (Numeric / Alphanumeric / Byte character classes, alphanumeric encoding values) are shared; only indicator widths and legality differ per symbology. `EncodingMode` also names Kanji, whose cells come from the shared `ShiftJisKanjiReverseTable`, and the analysis selects it for an eligible text when the caller sets `AllowKanji` |
| `SegmentDecoders` | Segment payload bit groups (numeric 10/7/4, alphanumeric 11/6, byte 8·count), the byte-charset heuristics (UTF-8 validation, BOM, Latin-1 widening) and the ECI designator reader (lifted from `QRBinaryDecoder` when rMQR became its second consumer, Phase 6) are identical across symbologies; the mode/count indicator framing that differs stays in each symbology's bitstream decoder (lifted out of `QRBinaryDecoder` in Phase 3 when the second consumer appeared) |
| `LuminanceConverter`, `PixelLayout`, `PerspectiveTransform` | Image preprocessing and geometry are symbology-independent. The luminance kernels are the seam the first-party image adapter feeds (see the package seam below) |
| `Point`, `Rectangle` | Plain geometry types |
| `ModuleRunScanner`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | Merging dark modules into horizontal runs depends only on the `IModuleMatrixView` shape, not the symbology. One implementation serves both the renderer's merged-run drawing path and the public `GetModuleRectangles` surface on all three data types, so the geometry the public API reports is by construction the geometry the renderer draws for an unstyled symbol (a styled one draws its finder as one pattern instead, which `GetModuleRectangles` still reports as the merged runs of its modules) |

**Per-symbology pipelines** (`Internals.StandardQR`, later `Internals.MicroQR`, `Internals.RmQR`), knowledge specific to one symbol format:

- Capacity / ECC / interleaving tables and version selection
- Mode indicator and character-count indicator widths
- Format (and version) information encoding and decoding
- Function pattern layout, data module placement, mask patterns and mask scoring
- Symbol detection and sampling in images

Dependency rule: shared code never references a symbology namespace; symbology namespaces never reference each other. Each symbology pipeline composes the shared primitives. `SymbologyDependencyTest` holds it on the library's build for every target framework, so code under a framework's `#if` is read where it compiles (a configuration's, `#if DEBUG` and a call to a `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` method such as `Debug.Assert`, only in the configuration the tests run in, Release on CI), and a build older than a source of the library is not read: its case is skipped, or fails on CI. A reference from a type of an internal namespace to a type of another symbology, or of a namespace below one, fails it however the source spelled it (a `using` of any kind, a global import, a linked file), be it a base type or interface, a signature, a local, a catch type, a generic constraint, an attribute or a type its arguments name, or a member or type a method's code names. Probe types in the test assembly hold each of these kinds to the reader, but a pinned local and a call through a function pointer, which only unsafe code makes. What compiles to no reference, a constant (an enum member among them) or a `nameof`, is left to a source check that reads each internal file's code, comments and `#if false` branches removed, for another symbology's namespace spelled out, a `using` of it, or a type qualified by its name; a constant reached by a spelling it does not know passes. Existing Standard QR code moves under `Internals.StandardQR` unchanged, no behavioral or algorithmic modification accompanies the move.

Two detection primitives were lifted from `Internals.StandardQR` to the shared `Internals.ImageDecoders` namespace when Micro QR image detection (Phase 4b) became their second consumer, exactly the trigger this document prescribed:

- `Binarizer`, generic binarization (moved out of `QRImageDecoder`): the histogram is counted once an image (a 256-bit tier, an ARM64 tier and a 128-bit tier count a block's two extreme values in registers, the ARM64 one spreading dense blocks over four sub-histograms; a scalar walk where no vector is accelerated), the threshold search and the grey levels read the histogram alone (the levels also give the luminance an edge is located at, halfway between them whether or not the image has grey pixels), and the inverted retry every image decoder makes mirrors the first polarity's bins instead of counting the negative and searches the threshold again on them, because two values with nothing between them tie at every split and `256 - threshold` is a different threshold on exactly a rendered symbol; all four tiers are held to one bin count, and the decisions and measurements are in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md)
- `FinderPatternFinder`, the 1:1:3:1:1 run-ratio scan and cross-checks; Micro QR and rMQR use the same finder pattern shape (single finder instead of three) via `FindCandidates`, which returns the cross-checked candidates and leaves to the decoder how many of them it decodes (a bounded number), Micro QR and rMQR both taking them in the order `RankByConfirmation` gives, the most confirmed first, while Standard QR keeps its best-three selection in `TryFind`; runs that miss the ratio by less than 1.5 px on every one of the five are measured again from grey levels (`GreyLevels`, taken from the threshold's own histogram) before they are refused, which is what reads anti-aliased edges at about 2 px/module. Each cross-check line is held to its own ratio; a column may be as much longer or shorter than its row as a finder in perspective is drawn (5/12 to 12/5), and past the row's own 40 % only when the rising diagonal reads too, which is what finds the finder a strong keystone stretches, in all three symbologies, for 30 more candidates over 540 two-level noise images (474 against 444) and the same 60 of them yielding a triple; the single-finder decoders' failures took 2 to 7 % longer (rMQR noise, a turned Micro QR), not traced further. A cross-check line the ratio refuses is read again by the distances between its edges of the same polarity (`IsFinderRatioByLikeEdges`), which a ring printed or read too thick or too thin keeps: within the row's own 40 %, with the row's shift sign, and with the rising diagonal asked too; its cost is in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling), and what it reads in each decoder's image envelope
- `LocalBinarizer`, a regional binarization (8 × 8 blocks, each pixel against the mean black point of the 5 × 5 blocks around its own), the regional pass of every image decoder ([Image decode passes](#image-decode-passes); `RegionalRetry` runs its two polarities, each binarized from its own pixels, so the three decoders share the order and the skips); it reads symbols under a lighting gradient, and why it is an added attempt rather than a replacement is in [standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling)
- `ImageDecodePasses`, the image decode passes themselves ([Image decode passes](#image-decode-passes)): one sequence and one set of rules for the three image decoders, each of which gives its symbol pass as a struct (`ISymbolPass`), so the calls stay direct. The midpoint pass is a switch of that struct, off for Standard QR. Until 2026-09-29 each decoder ran its own copy of the sequence, Micro QR's and rMQR's line for line; moving them changed no read and no status over the image decode sweep and the real-image corpus
- `ImageView`, one reading of an image as a pass reads it (pixels, size, threshold, grey levels and the level an edge is located at), which the image decoders' stages hand down as one argument where they took five or six. The stages that measure (finder sizes, grids, samplers) still take the pieces they read, so each says what it reads and a test can call it alone. It came in on 2026-09-29, when up to 16 parameters a stage carried the image through Standard QR's search.
- `SymbolGeometry`, where a symbol that read lies in the image: the corners of the mapping that decoded it (`SymbolCorners`), which every image decoder reports with a successful read, and whether a point lies inside them (`Contains`, `AnyContains`), which the Micro QR and rMQR scans ask of a later candidate after a read that does not fit the destination (below)
- `AttemptStatus` and `SearchResult`, how the image decoders read a decode attempt's status and which result a search of many attempts reports.
  - The status classes are written once: a read or a read too long for the destination is terminal, a verdict on the content settles the symbol, and a grid past its format information is worth refining. So is how far an attempt got.
  - A search reports its failure by one of two rules. Standard QR reports the main path's attempt at each level of its search, the attempt it would make alone, unless another settles. Micro QR and rMQR report the failure that went furthest, since they try many grids of one finder and none of them is first.
  - Standard QR stays on its own rule because its format word names no version. A grid sampled at a guessed dimension reads near-random bits there, and about half of all 15-bit words lie within three bits of a valid word, so the grid gets past the format information by chance and fails at Reed-Solomon with its own dimension's version. Moved to the furthest failure on 2026-09-30 to try it, 51 of 80 symbols with their format information destroyed reported `DataUncorrectable` one version too small, where they had reported `FormatInformationInvalid` with their own version; no read changed. Micro QR's format word names the symbol and rMQR's the version, so there a grid of a size other than the one the word names is refused at the format information.
  - Where a search stops stays the decoder's. A terminal result ends the passes in all three. Inside a pass, Standard QR stops at a settled result, and Micro QR's and rMQR's scans only at a read, since another symbol in the image may read.
  - Standard QR takes a level's result only at the level's first attempt that does not settle, and returns a settled attempt as it is, which either rule reports when only unsettled attempts came before it. On the WebAssembly interpreter every result operation is a call: taken ahead of each level, the results cost a version 6 read at 4 px/module about 6 µs of 136, and nothing measurable compiled (2026-10-01).
  - Micro QR and rMQR both stop a finder candidate at a terminal result, a read that does not fit the destination included ([microqr-decoder.md](microqr-decoder.md#decisions), [rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md#decisions)), and go on to the other candidates, skipping one inside the symbol that read: symbols do not overlap, so it is a finder-like pattern in that symbol's own data. Searched in full after the read, such a candidate cost about 4 to 105 times a sized call on the rMQR renders found with one and about 5 to 70 times on the Micro QR ones, the low ends on turned and noisy renders; skipped, a destination too short cost at worst 1.5 times a sized call on 577 Micro QR and 585 such renders of rMQR (2026-10-01).
  - Until 2026-09-29 each decoder wrote these out itself, the furthest-failure ranking twice.
- Not shared, on purpose: the mirror retry. The three decoders read a mirrored capture, whose finders are the same and whose data is transposed, three ways, each for a reason:
  - Standard QR transposes its sampled grid in place, since its matrix level reads the modules two at a time along the placement runs, which a transposed view would not keep contiguous.
  - Micro QR reads its grid through a transposed view, since its matrix level reads every module through one; one helper does it for every grid.
  - rMQR samples again with the frame's axes swapped, since a transposed rMQR grid is no rMQR grid.
- `ModuleBoundaryReader`, the grid of a crisp axis-aligned symbol below 1.75 px/module as a table of module boundaries read off the timing patterns and the finder's own lines, instead of a fitted transform; each symbology says where its timing lines run and how they end (a far finder for Standard QR, the quiet zone for Micro QR and rMQR, with rMQR's three-module alignment and corner runs allowed on the line)
- `ConcentricCentroid`, a concentric pattern's centre as the centroid of its centre square's darkness in a window along the symbol's axes that ends inside the light ring, to a fraction of a pixel where thresholded runs give half a pixel; it needs the grey levels (on a two-level image it leaves the centre alone) and refines the three Standard QR finders, its alignment patterns and mesh nodes, the Micro QR finder and the rMQR finder and sub-finder
- `PerspectiveGridSampler`, a square module grid read through one projective transform, each module centre's pixel against the threshold, with 256-bit and 128-bit tiers: Standard QR's four-point, parallelogram and finders' frame grids, and Micro QR's perspective search. It was `QRImageDecoder.SampleGrid` until 2026-09-29, and Micro QR called it there, against the dependency rule; `SymbologyDependencyTest` now holds the rule over the built library and the source. rMQR keeps its own sampler, since its grid is not square and has an affine tier
- `LuminanceSampler`, luminance interpolated between pixel centres, for the coverage reading: on an image with grey levels a grid that failed is read again with each module's centre against the midpoint of the two levels, where the first reading takes one pixel against the global threshold (Standard QR its global grid, Micro QR a grid that read its format word exactly, rMQR a grid that read its format information), and decoded only when that changes a module
- `FinderAxisEstimator`, the finder-local module scale for all three symbologies (dark-light-dark runs that pair edges of the same polarity, so ink spread and erosion do not scale it; for Standard QR on an image with grey levels the same pairing to sub-pixel edges, where the luminance interpolated along the line crosses halfway between the two levels, fine enough to measure how the module size changes along a finder line under perspective) and single-finder axis recovery for Micro QR and rMQR (an axis fitted to a 90-direction sweep, then the sweep's separated minima); lifted from the Micro QR image decoder when rMQR image detection (Phase 7) became its second consumer, and the Standard QR finder-to-finder measurement folded into it in 2026-09
- `FinderOutline`, a 7 × 7 finder's own frame, shear included, off the inner edges of its light ring, where the angular sweep gives square frames; rMQR measures a finder in strong perspective with it, and `ProjectiveFit`, the least-squares homography from point correspondences accumulated as moments with nothing stored, fits its traced perimeter ([rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md)) and places the Standard QR mesh nodes for versions 7 to 13 that are not searched or not found ([standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#piecewise-mesh-version-7)); the image side is moved and scaled to unit size first, because raw pixel sums lose the fit from about 4,000 px out

### Image decode passes

The three image decoders read an image in the same sequence of passes, run by one shared driver (`ImageDecodePasses`); only Micro QR and rMQR have the last one, the midpoint pass. Each pass decides how the image is read, then runs the symbology's own pipeline on it. The global and midpoint passes set a threshold on the luminance; the regional pass instead produces an image binarized region by region. A pass runs only when the passes before it read nothing, and the rules below say which results end the sequence early. The per-symbology pipelines are drawn in the spec-to-code maps: [Standard QR](standardqr-spec-map.md#decoding-pipeline), [Micro QR](microqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling), [rMQR](rmqr-spec-map.md#image-detection-and-sampling).

```
Luminance ──> histogram, counted once
├─ Global, positive   Otsu threshold ──> symbol pass
├─ Global, negative   the image inverted; Otsu threshold of the mirrored histogram ──> symbol pass
├─ Regional           each pixel against the mean black point of the blocks around its own,
│                     positive then negative ──> symbol pass each
└─ Midpoint           Micro QR and rMQR, for each polarity whose global pass found no finder candidate:
                      halfway between its two grey levels ──> full finder sweep ──> symbology pipeline

Symbol pass
├─ Standard QR        finder triple ──> symbology pipeline
│                     the triple comes from a strided row scan, which also scans the rows it skipped when it
│                     selects no triple, or selects a doubtful one after setting once-seen candidates aside
└─ Micro QR, rMQR     strided finder scan ──> symbology pipeline
                      nothing read: full finder sweep ──> symbology pipeline
```

- The rules count attempts. Each global pass is one symbol pass. The regional pass runs one symbol pass per polarity, and the midpoint pass one full sweep per polarity that qualifies; in both, the positive goes first.
- A read ends the sequence: nothing runs after the attempt that made it. A read here includes text that was decoded but did not fit the destination.
- A verdict on the content (`UnmappedCharacter`, `UnsupportedContent`) means the symbol was seen, and it ends the sequence the same way. There are two exceptions:
  - After a verdict from the global positive pass, the global negative pass still runs, and a read there wins.
  - A verdict from the strided scan of a Micro QR or rMQR symbol pass does not skip that pass's full sweep, which can find another symbol that reads.
- The full sweep of a Micro QR or rMQR symbol pass does not decode a candidate its strided scan already decoded without settling: the same candidate, image and threshold give the same outcome. The sweep still tries only its own first eight, so a skipped one is not replaced by the ninth, and when the strided scan settled on a verdict nothing is skipped.
- When one attempt reaches more than one result, the symbology's own rule decides which it reports (see its map).
- The regional pass is skipped when a side of the image is 32 px or less, which leaves too few blocks for one neighbourhood, or when the image holds only 0 and 255. Within the pass, a polarity is not decoded when its binarization leaves every pixel in the class its global threshold gave it.
- The regional pass reads an image with only two levels, so it has no grey levels, and no stage that needs them runs in it.
- The midpoint pass needs grey levels, and it is skipped when the midpoint equals the global threshold.
- The global threshold can land inside a wide noisy background. Levels squeezed to 100-170 with ±24 of noise, the symbol a small part of the image, put Otsu near 165, inside the light background, and in 65 of 65 such failures the finder was never a candidate (measured on rMQR, 2026-09-28; the threshold is every symbology's).
- When no pass reads the symbol or gives a verdict, the result carries the global positive pass's diagnostics. For Micro QR and rMQR, those are the diagnostics of its strided scan.

Why the passes are ordered this way:
- Every pass after the first runs only on an image the passes before it failed to read. An image the global threshold reads therefore pays for nothing else, and the buffer for the inverted image is rented only after that failure.
- The negative needs no second count, because its histogram is the positive's mirrored (`Binarizer` above).
- The regional pass is an added attempt, not a replacement for the global threshold ([standardqr-decoder.md](standardqr-decoder.md#image-detection-and-sampling)).
- A verdict ends only what could not change the answer. A rule stated for the symbol has to hold for the image: stopping a Micro QR or rMQR search at a verdict would also stop it for every other symbol in the image, and a strided verdict that skipped the full sweep lost 20 to 24 readable neighbours in about 490 pairs of an unmapped symbol beside a low-density readable one. So a symbol holding an unmapped Kanji cell cost 2 to 19 ms against microseconds for a mappable one (2026-09-23, before the failure-path work made those searches faster), which is the price.
- The midpoint pass is for a finder the global threshold cannot see. Edge greys pull that threshold toward light, and a blurred finder's light ring can keep too few pixels above it; halfway between the two levels the ring reads its width. It runs last, so a symbol the regional pass reads never pays for it. Since the cross-checks read like edges, most such finders are found at the global threshold; among bilinear upscales of every version at 2 to 3.2 px/module, only Micro QR M1 and rMQR R7x43 and R7x77 still needed it. Standard QR has none: its sweep read 4,799 of 4,800 bilinear renders at 2 to 3.5 px/module without one, and the one left was unread before the passes were shared too (2026-09-29). Adding it would be an accuracy change of its own, measured by the sweep, for an input class that needs it.
- The finder search widens in two different ways because the trigger to widen has to be a question about the symbol. Standard QR's search can ask one itself: did the strided rows give it a triple that is not in doubt? A single-finder scan cannot ask anything like that, so the Micro QR and rMQR decoders ask instead whether the strided scan read the symbol ([rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md#decisions), finder candidate scan).

### Package architecture

Since 2.0.0 the library ships as three NuGet packages built from two assemblies in this repository (the core split, 2026-09):

| Package | Assembly | Contents | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FeatherQR` | `FeatherQR.dll` | Generators, decoders, data types, options, segmentation, `ModuleRect` geometry, the luminance kernels | Nothing on net8.0 and net10.0; `System.Memory` (netstandard2.0) and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe` (netstandard2.1) |
| `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.dll` | `SymbolRenderer`, the `SKCanvas` extensions, the image builders, `IconData` and shapes, `SKBitmap` decoding as extension members on the core decoders | `FeatherQR`, `SkiaSharp` |
| `SkiaSharp.QrCode` | none | An empty compatibility metapackage: the ID the library shipped under through 1.x keeps restoring | `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` |

Namespaces follow the packages: `FeatherQR` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`, with the internals of each under `FeatherQR.Internals` and `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals`. The former `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Image` sub-namespace is folded into `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`; one namespace per package is the cheapest shape to explain in a major that changes every `using` line anyway.

**Dependency rules.**

- The core references no package that is not a BCL shim, and the shims only where the framework lacks `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`. Two guards hold this: `CoreAssemblyDependencyTest` reads the core assembly's references from metadata for every target framework, and `tools/check_package_deps.cs` reads the packed nuspecs (see "Package graph" below). A dependency that slips in passes build and test and fails both.
- The rendering package reaches the core through the public surface, plus the enumerated `InternalsVisibleTo` uses recorded below ("Package seam"). The core never references the rendering package.
- Skia types appear only in the rendering assembly. Inside `namespace FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` the simple name `SkiaSharp` binds to that namespace, so `using SkiaSharp;` sits above the file-scoped namespace declaration and qualified `SkiaSharp.SKBitmap` spellings are not used.
- No unified `Create(symbology, ...)` entry point is ever added. The three generators, decoders and data types do not reference each other, and that is what makes trimming precise: a consumer that uses one symbology keeps one symbology.

**What the split buys, measured.** With `PublishTrimmed` (`TrimMode=full`) on a console app, measured on 2026-09-04 on the pre-split assembly:

| Consumer profile | Trimmed managed assembly |
|---:|---:|
| QR encode only | 95 KB |
| All three symbologies, encode | 153 KB |
| All three, encode and decode, including `TryDecode(SKBitmap)` | 229 KB |
| Untrimmed net10.0 | 384 KB |

The managed assembly was never the cost. `libSkiaSharp` is 11.9 MB per RID, cannot be trimmed, and is deployed whether or not a single Skia call survives; only a package boundary removes it, and only for consumers that reference `FeatherQR` alone. A per-symbology package split was rejected: it would save untrimmed consumers roughly 100 to 130 KB, cost a four-package core with a public surface for the shared kernels, and buy nothing for trimmed consumers, who already get the numbers above.

**What "lightweight" means.** The brand word is defined as zero dependencies in the core, zero allocations on the hot paths, and trim and NativeAOT safety. It is not a claim about assembly bytes: at 300 to 390 KB the core is larger than single-symbology libraries because it carries three symbologies, the decoders and the SIMD tiers. The README states the definition in its first lines so the name never has to be defended against a byte count.

### Package seam: what the rendering package reaches through `InternalsVisibleTo`

`FeatherQR` grants `InternalsVisibleTo` to `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp`. The rule is that a third-party renderer must be writable against the public surface alone, so every internal the first-party renderer still uses is listed here with either its public replacement or the reason it stays internal. The list is checked by building the rendering project with the grant removed: whatever fails to compile is the list.

| Internal | Used by | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| `LuminanceConverter.Convert(pixels, width, height, rowBytes, PixelLayout, premultipliedAlpha, luminance)`, `PixelLayout`, `ImageDimensions.TryGetPixelCount` | `Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` and the `SKBitmap` decode overloads | **Stays internal, by decision (core split Phase 2).** The public decode seam is `TryDecodeImage(luminance, width, height, ...)`, which already lets a third-party adapter decode from any image library; what it does not get is the SIMD conversion and the white-compositing behavior for free, and no such adapter has been asked for. Publishing the kernels is a one-way door (removing an API needs a major, adding one needs a minor), so they stay internal until a concrete request exists. The `TryDecodeImage` documentation states the white-compositing expectation so a hand-written converter does not composite transparent pixels against black. The rendering package keeps a single-entry adapter, `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp.Internals.BitmapLuminanceConverter` (`SKColorType` to `PixelLayout` over `SKPixmap.GetPixelSpan()`), so promoting the seam later is a visibility change, not a redesign |
| `RmQRConstants.QuietZoneModules`, `RmQRConstants.IsValidVersion` | `RmQRCodeImageBuilder` | **Replaced.** The builder reads the specified quiet zone from `default(RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions).QuietZoneSize`, which is the same constant behind a public property, and validates a requested version with `Enum.IsDefined`, which the contiguous `RmQRVersion` enum makes exact |
| `IModuleMatrixView`, `StandardQrMatrixView` / `MicroQRMatrixView` / `RmQRMatrixView`, `ModuleRunEnumerator<TView>` | `SymbolRenderer` merged-run and per-module drawing loops | **Stays internal, by decision.** The public equivalent is `GetModuleRectangles` / `TryGetModuleRectangles` on the three data types, built on the same `ModuleRunScanner`, so a third-party renderer draws exactly the geometry the first-party one does. The first-party renderer keeps the streaming enumerator because it draws each run as it is found with no rectangle buffer; going through the public surface would add a `GetModuleRectanglesMaxCount()`-sized rental per render (up to ~15,700 rectangles for version 40) to the one path that is measured as allocation-free. Exposing the struct-generic view machinery itself would freeze an implementation detail as API for one caller |

### Package graph: what each nuspec declares

Three packages ship from one `dotnet pack` at one lockstep version (`Directory.Build.props`): `FeatherQR` (core), `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` (rendering, depends on `FeatherQR` and `SkiaSharp`) and `SkiaSharp.QrCode` (an empty compatibility metapackage that depends on `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` and carries no `lib/`). `tools/check_package_deps.cs` opens the packed nupkgs and asserts the exact dependency group of every target framework after every pack in CI; the expectation is a literal table in the tool, so a change to the graph is a diff someone accepts on purpose.

**The core is dependency-free where the framework carries `Span<T>`, `ArrayPool<T>` and `Unsafe`, and depends on the BCL shims where it does not.** net8.0 and net10.0 groups are empty; netstandard2.0 depends on `System.Memory` and netstandard2.1 on `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe`. Before the split these arrived transitively through SkiaSharp, which is why removing SkiaSharp broke only the netstandard builds. "Zero dependencies" in the package description means this.

**Transitive pinning is off for the whole repository.** `CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled` promotes every transitive package that has a `PackageVersion` entry into the nuspec as a direct dependency, which for 1.x meant `SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Win32` and `.macOS` beside `SkiaSharp`, and would have meant `SkiaSharp` and the native assets beside `FeatherQR.SkiaSharp` in the metapackage. The promotion changes nothing a consumer resolves (SkiaSharp brings its native assets itself) but makes the package declare a graph it does not have and the assertion above meaningless. The other half of the feature, forcing a transitive version floor on applications, has no use here: the test, benchmark, playground and sample projects are not shipped products, `NuGetAudit` reports a vulnerable resolution, and a direct `PackageReference` raises a transitive version when one ever needs raising. One setting in `Directory.Packages.props` is therefore simpler than a per-project exception that every future packable project would have to remember.

### Public API direction

Each symbology gets its own generator entry point with symbology-typed version and error-correction parameters.

**One naming rule decides every public name in both packages.** A prefix says which symbology — `QR` for Standard QR, `MicroQR`, `RmQR` — and no prefix means the type is shared by all three. A noun that literally denotes *a code* keeps the `{Sym}Code` form (`QRCodeData`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator`, `RmQRCodeDecodeInfo`); everything else, enums and ranges and strategies, takes the short prefix (`QREccLevel`, `QRSegmentation`, `QRVersionRange`). Three-letter acronyms are Pascal-cased (`Ecc`, `Eci`, `Bom`). The rule was implicit while Micro QR and rMQR were built, which is why those two already followed it; 2.0.0 applied it to the Standard QR types written first (`ECCLevel`, `QRCodeSegmentation`, `QRCodeVersionRange`) and to the shared types that had taken the `QRCode` prefix while meaning the whole family (`QRCodeDecodeStatus` became `DecodeStatus`, and in the rendering package `QRCodeRenderer` and `QRCodeImageBuilderBase<TSelf>` became `SymbolRenderer` and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, the word both standards use). The defect the rule removes is that double meaning: `QRCode` cannot be Standard QR in one type name and the family in the next. `QRCodeExtensions` became `SKCanvasExtensions` under the neighbouring BCL habit of naming an extension holder after what it extends.

**The method name repeats what the class already says, so it says nothing.** `QRCodeGenerator.CreateQrCode`, `MicroQRCodeGenerator.CreateMicroQRCode` and `RmQRCodeGenerator.CreateRmQRCode` are all `Create` since 2.0.0. That also deletes rather than answers the `Qr` versus `QR` casing question those method names carried, and it is why the rule needs no clause about it.

**Options live in a per-symbology options struct, and since 2.0.0 that is the only way to configure a generator.** `QRCodeGeneratorOptions`, `MicroQRCodeGeneratorOptions` and `RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions` are `readonly record struct`s passed by `in`, so the allocation-free entry points stay allocation-free. The parameter list overloads that 1.1.1 released were frozen through 1.2.0 (exact signatures, exceptions and messages, never another parameter) and removed in 2.0.0; rMQR never had them. The rule exists because the parameter list shape had already failed on rMQR before it shipped, at 10 methods with up to 9 parameters, with one option escaping into method names: `EciMode` could not be added positionally without disturbing the existing order, so `CreateRmQRCodeWithEci` and two siblings were added instead, doubling the method count while Standard QR expressed the same concept as an ordinary parameter.

**The reshaping was possible only because of a release window.** No rMQR API had ever been in a NuGet package, so its surface could be fixed by deletion at zero compatibility cost; Standard QR and Micro QR had no such freedom and kept their released overloads. Package validation against the last published package is what enforced the difference (`EnablePackageValidation` with `PackageValidationBaselineVersion`), and the baseline was then pinned at 1.1.1 for the rest of the 1.x line rather than moving with each release, so the surface 1.2.0 added was never covered by one; it is unset on the 2.0.0 packages until 2.0.0 ships. A minor release cannot reopen that window; the 2.0.0 major is what let the deprecation cycle finish, and anything wanting the same change again waits for the next major.

**Package validation only polices the half of a change that breaks somebody, so the exported surface is also held to a listing in the repository.** Validation answers "would this break a caller who compiled against the last release", and a new public member never does: it lands unreviewed, which is the wrong default for a library whose next release is a rename. `src/FeatherQR/PublicAPI.approved.txt` and `src/FeatherQR.SkiaSharp/PublicAPI.approved.txt` record every exported type and member of the two assemblies and are regenerated by `tools/check_public_api.cs`, gated on pull requests and again at release. A listing only gates what it prints: properties carried no `abstract` / `virtual` / `override` until 2026-09-13, so `FinderPatternShape.RequiresAntialiasing` turning abstract, which stops an already-compiled subclass from loading, passed the check as "unchanged" until the same helper was used for both accessors and methods. Changing the surface is therefore a diff someone accepts deliberately, and the 2.0.0 reshaping arrives as one reviewable file rather than as a claim in a pull request description.

**On a builder option, `null` means the option is absent and never "the default value".** A default that has a name is passed by name: `RectangleModuleShape.Default` and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` for plain shapes, `SKColors.Black` and `SKColors.White` for the two colours. Through 2.0.0-preview.2 the fluent setters spelled those states as `null` as well, which bought a second spelling of a state that already had one and let `WithColors`'s optional parameters read as "leave the rest alone" while behaving as "reset the rest" — appending `.WithColors(clearColor: …)` to a chain discarded the colours an earlier call had set. 2.0.0 made the colours and both shape setters non-nullable, cut `WithColors` down to the two colours a symbol always has (both required), and added `WithCodeColor` / `WithBackgroundColor` / `WithClearColor` so one colour can be changed on its own. The nulls that survive are the ones that name an absence rather than a value: no gradient, no icon, and no clear colour of its own, which leaves the padding following the background. **The rule is about a default that stands in for a value, not about optional parameters as such.** `WithModuleShape(shape, sizePercent = 1.0f)` and `WithFormat(format, quality = 100)` were reviewed against it on 2026-09-14 and left as they are: their defaults are the values themselves, written in the signature and in the parameter documentation, so omitting the argument does what it reads as doing, and a second call to either setter is a rewrite of the first rather than an adjustment to it. **`WithFinderPatternShape` was the row that had to be measured rather than reasoned about, and the first measurement was too narrow.** Omitting it is not the same code path as naming the square — the finders are drawn with the modules, and `RectangleFinderPatternShape.Default` is substituted only once the modules are styled, which is the rule that styling never reaches a finder pattern — so it read as a third state, *auto*. In raster output the two spellings are pixel-identical across symbologies, canvas sizes and background alphas. They once differed, invisibly, by one step of one channel in tens of pixels under a gradient over a translucent background, because the finder pass composited through a layer and the merged-run path did not; with the layer gone (recorded below) they are 0 pixels apart there too, measured at 300 to 900 pixels square. So the null was a second spelling of a named value, and the merged-run path is an implementation detail the builder keeps for callers who never ask for a shape. In SVG the two spellings are still not element-identical, and cannot be: naming the square routes the finders through the finder pass, which writes five rectangles each, while omitting it leaves them to the merged-run path, thirty elements more on Standard QR at every alpha. What was a defect until the finder drawing changed (below) is that the documents also *looked* different; the equivalence claim is about pixels and belongs to raster and SVG alike, not about the element list. The `SKCanvas.Render` extensions keep `null` for every option, and `SymbolRenderer.Render` for every option but the two colours. For the shapes and for every parameter of the extensions the reason is the language rather than the rule — a C# optional parameter needs a constant default, and a shape instance is not one, while `SKColor` has no constant spelling for black and `default` is transparent. It was not the reason for `SymbolRenderer.Render`'s `codeColor` and `backgroundColor`, which were *required* parameters typed `SKColor?`: nothing but consistency with the extensions that forward to them kept those nullable, and that the pair was never revisited showed in their documentation, which described them as omittable until the 2.0.0 review corrected it. Since 2026-09-13 they are `SKColor`, and the extensions resolve an omitted colour to black or white before forwarding, as they already did for the clear colour. A colourless overload beside each of the three, defaulting to black on white, was the other candidate and was compiled before being declined: it binds every positional and named spelling unambiguously except `default, default`, and on Standard QR, the only overload with an `IconData?` parameter, it lets the old `Render(canvas, area, data, null, null)` compile by taking the two nulls as `iconData` and `moduleShape`, pixel-identical and undiagnosed, a migration the compiler could then not hand to the caller; Micro QR and rMQR would refuse the same call, since the second `null` would have to reach a `float`. It lost on the caller's experience rather than on that: the `SKCanvas` a caller holds never assumes a colour, since every Skia draw call takes its paint, omission already exists one layer up in both the builders and the extensions, and a second signature per symbology is one more to keep in step for every option added later. What a caller now writes under a gradient is a code colour that is not used; that is `SKPaint`'s own model, a shader taking precedence over the colour, and the parameter documentation says so, with the two cases where the colour is painted after all: a gradient whose direction is `None`, and no gradient. A fill type that would make the two exclusive was designed and declined on 2026-09-14, because the builders have to keep the colour and the gradient as two states for a caller that decides between them at run time, so only the static surface would have taken the fill and the two surfaces would have modelled the same thing differently. For the colours and the module shape the rule changed what a caller can write and nothing about what comes out, since the renderer already resolved each `null` to exactly the values the builder now holds; the finder shape was, until the finder drawing changed (below), the one where the *substitute* a caller reaches for, rather than the rule, could change the output, and only in SVG.

**A finder shape draws its dark modules only; the light ring is a hole, never a paint and never an erase.** Until 2.0.0 a `FinderPatternShape` drew the outer square dark and then painted the ring light over it, which is wrong on any background below alpha 255 (the ring came out as a translucent light over dark), so the renderer wrapped each finder in a `SaveLayer` and let the shape erase the ring with `SKBlendMode.Clear`. That is correct on a raster surface and inexpressible for `SKSvgCanvas`, which dropped the whole layer: the SVG document had no finder patterns at all, a symbol nothing can scan, on every symbology and by two routes, an explicit `WithFinderPatternShape` and any styled module set (styling substitutes a solid square finder). The condition was exactly `background alpha < 255`; 254 was enough. Measured before the change with this library's own decoder on browser-rasterised SVG, Standard QR at 512x512: the four non-opaque cases (alpha 254 and 128 with a named square, alpha 128 and 0 with styled modules) all failed and the two opaque ones read. The fix is geometry rather than erasure: the ring is a hole in what the shape draws, so it shows whatever the renderer already put beneath it, the background at any alpha, with no layer and no blend mode, and both canvas kinds get the same drawing. **Which geometry expresses the hole is decided by what `SKSvgCanvas` can write**, since it flattens a path into thousands of quadratic segments and writes a rectangle or an oval as one element: the square finder is four bands and a centre rectangle; a circle's ring is a one-module stroke of its middle oval, which is exactly the region between the 5x5 and 7x7 ovals because a circle's offset curve is another circle, with the centre a filled oval; and the two rounded shapes need an even-odd path for their ring, whose radii differ per contour, but keep any oval centre out of it. Measured on a 512x512 Standard QR of "https://githu" at ECC M, 29 modules, since the figures move with the module count: a circle finder's document is 5.8 KB drawn this way against 49.9 KB as one even-odd path, and the rounded-circle one 35.7 KB against 50.4 KB. The stroke holds only where the cells are square, because one stroke width cannot be one module on both axes, so a shape handed a non-square rect falls back to the path; the renderer never hands it one. The two `Draw` overloads that carried a light colour or paint went with the layer, since a shape that painted the ring could only be made right by erasing; the contract is now the one method, dark modules only. The finder's antialiasing follows the finder shape rather than the module shape in the same change, so a square finder beside round modules stays crisp; `RequiresAntialiasing` is `abstract`, as `ModuleShape`'s is, because the renderer now assigns it in both directions and an inherited default would silently mean "draw my curves aliased". The lesson is the one the rule above already states from the decoder's side: a finder pattern is read as runs of dark and light, and the light runs are the background, so they should be drawn as the background and not as a colour that has to match it.

**The listing is read from every target framework, which turned an assumption into a fact.** The library builds for four, nothing had ever compared them, and the claim that no exported member is framework-conditional lived only in a tool comment. It held when the gate was introduced, and a build where it stops holding now fails instead of shipping. Two renderers of the same surface exist on purpose, the reflection one behind the Playground's API page and the metadata one behind the gate, and their agreeing line for line is what keeps either from drifting unnoticed.

The type name is `{consuming generator}Options`, mechanically, so no reader has to work out which struct belongs to which generator. This follows the BCL habit of naming an options bag after its consumer (`JsonSerializerOptions` for `JsonSerializer`) and leaves `{X}DecoderOptions` free under the same rule.

Consequences worth stating here rather than three times:

- **The `options` parameter carries a default on every entry point, and could not while the parameter lists existed.** rMQR had `in RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions options = default` from the start because its parameter list versions were deleted before release; on Standard QR and Micro QR a defaulted options parameter would have made `Create(text, ecc)` ambiguous between the two sets, so callers wrote `QRCodeGeneratorOptions.Default with { ... }` explicitly until 2.0.0 removed the other set. Sizing never had the problem: `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` was always the only sizing overload, so its options parameter was defaulted from the start. The asymmetry was a consequence of the released surface rather than a preference, which is why removing that surface was enough to end it.

- **`default(T)` must be the complete default configuration**, since it is what an omitted argument sends. Any member whose documented default is not the zero value stores an offset from that default, not a `value + 1` sentinel, so that writing the default explicitly produces the same value as not writing it and the generated equality does not report two identical option sets as different. `QuietZoneSize` is the only such member today, and its correct default differs per symbology (4, 2, 2), which is also why one shared options type is not expressible.
- **Options are not shared across symbologies.** The intersection of the three option sets is one `int` with three different correct defaults: `Version` is a different type in each, Micro QR has no ECI, and rMQR's fit options mean nothing elsewhere. A shared type would carry members invalid for two thirds of its uses and reject them at run time instead of at compile time.
- **The error correction level stays a required parameter and is deliberately not an option.** It is the only input with no correct default: L and H differ by roughly 4x in capacity, and choosing between capacity and robustness is the caller's decision, not the library's. Putting it in the options struct would force `default(T)` to encode that choice silently, which contradicts the rule above. The line this draws is that the required arguments say *what symbol you want* (the text and how robust it must be) while the options say *how to encode and render it*. The image builders do default it to `M`, which is right for a "just give me a picture" entry point and wrong for the generator.
- **A version *range* exists only where versions are totally ordered.** `QRVersionRange` (1-40) and `MicroQRVersionRange` (M1-M4) subsume the single requested version, with a pinned version as the degenerate `Exactly` case; `null` and `int?` convert implicitly so an optional version needs no branch at the call site. rMQR has no range because its 32 versions have no min/max relation, and constrains fit with `RmQRFitStrategy` and `RmQRHeight` instead.

**The `string` convenience overloads went with them.** `string` converts implicitly to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, so `Create("text", ecc)` still binds; what the overloads added was a parameter name (`plainText` rather than `textSpan`) and a second row in every IntelliSense list. They were kept while their released counterparts pinned the shape and dropped in 2.0.0 with them, which also ended the asymmetry where only Standard QR had a `string` destination overload. Every generator is now two `Create` methods, span and span-plus-destination, plus `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`.

That reasoning was recorded as holding on all four target frameworks, and it holds on three. The conversion is compiler-synthesized rather than an operator on `System.String`, and when `ReadOnlySpan<T>` arrives from the `System.Memory` package instead of the framework — the netstandard2.0 asset, which is what .NET Framework consumers bind — only C# 14 synthesizes it. Every language version through 13 reports `CS1503` there. The lesson is that "converts implicitly" is a property of the span's provenance and the consumer's compiler, not of the target framework, and that a claim about consumer compilation has to be measured from a consumer project rather than reasoned about from the library's own build, which compiles at C# 14 and therefore proves nothing. The same measurement found the larger half: `init` accessors need C# 9, so on the netstandard2.0 (default C# 7.3) and netstandard2.1 (default C# 8.0) assets the option structs were unconfigurable once the parameter lists were gone. Each of the three, and `IconData`, now carries a constructor for that audience, which is why an option settable only through an object initializer is a defect the shape tests check for.

Decoding: matrix-level entry points are symbology-explicit (matrix size alone distinguishes Micro QR 11–17 from Standard 21–177, but rectangular input needs width/height). Image-level decoding keeps Standard-QR-only scanning as the default; additional symbologies are opt-in so the existing detection hot path keeps its performance characteristics.

**A successful image decode also says where the symbol was.** Every `*DecodeInfo` carries `Corners`, a `SymbolCorners` of four `ImagePoint`s (both shared, library-built record structs): the outer corners of the module area, quiet zone excluded, in the input's *continuous* pixel coordinates — (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the top-left pixel, so the values plot directly in SkiaSharp, a canvas or System.Drawing. No shift is applied at the boundary: the finder centres every mapping is anchored on come from run boundaries with an exclusive end and are already in that convention, so a symbol drawn from pixel 48 reports 48.0 (the first implementation added half a pixel on the theory that the samplers' `(int)(x + 0.5f)` meant "integer = pixel centre"; a tenth-of-a-pixel test on the finder-anchored corners is what caught it). The corners are named in the symbol's own frame (`TopLeft` is beside the finder that defines the symbol's top-left, wherever the camera put it), which is what lets one quadrilateral report rotation and, through reversed winding, mirroring; the square decoders retry a mirrored capture by transposing the sampled matrix, so the one bit they have to carry out is whether that retry won, while rMQR's frames swap axes and its transform is already in symbol order. The value is populated only on `Success`: a matrix decode has no image, and a failed image decode located nothing a caller should draw. It is an estimate from the fitted geometry, and the stated bound follows how much each decoder infers. Standard QR (three finders plus an alignment pattern, and for the mesh path a transform re-anchored on the mesh's far lattice node) holds half a module for flat, rotated, mirrored and keystoned captures at the tilts the corner tests run (12 % on versions 2 and 5, 6 to 8 % on 7 and 10, 5 to 6 % from version 14 up; the 8 px per module test scene decodes further on most versions, to 15 to 17 % on 2 and 5 and 10 % on 7 and 30, and holds the bound there too) — **and at 8 px per module or more**. Below that density the bound belongs in pixels, not modules: the bottom-right corner is anchored on the alignment pattern, whose centre the finder resolves to roughly a pixel at any module size, so the error is near-constant in pixels (measured on version 2 over every rotation: 4.09 px at 6 px per module, 3.63 at 8, 3.94 at 12) while the module it is divided by shrinks — 0.68 module at 6 px per module against 0.33 at 12 (measured before the alignment centre was refined to a fraction of a pixel on images with grey levels, 2026-09-25, and not measured since). A second loosening is structural rather than a matter of scale: whenever the bottom-right alignment pattern is not located, `BuildGridTransform` falls back to the finders-only parallelogram quad that version 1 always gets, and error correction still returns `Success`, so a version-2-and-up symbol with one damaged module over that pattern reports an ordinary result with that corner up to about a module and a half out. The public contract states both, because nothing in `QRCodeDecodeInfo` tells a caller which fit ran. Micro QR and rMQR fit from a single finder and hold half a module flat and at right angles (rMQR also at the one oblique angle tested): an oblique Micro QR rotation is reported at whichever 1° axis angle first decodes, and the finder sweep's run-length score is flat for ±3 to 4° around the truth, so the winner is routinely 1 to 2° off and the far corners measure 0.2 to 0.9 module at any pixel scale; a Micro QR keystone through the same search measures 0.55 to 0.76 module at 5 to 8 % and 1.03 mirrored at 8 %; and an rMQR grid anchored on the sub-finder reads a keystone through error correction without following it, so its far corners carry the residual: at 8 px per module over every version (re-measured 2026-09-28), 1.27 module with the top edge shortened 2 % a side, 1.55 to 1.86 at 3 to 8 % (worst R17x43) and 2.10 at 10 % (R11x27), 0.67 or less with the left edge shortened to 4 %, while the stronger keystones, which only a grid traced round the symbol's perimeter reads, measure 0.16 or less with the left edge shortened and 0.59 and 0.47 with the top shortened 12 and 15 %. The contract says "about a module" for those and "about two modules" for an rMQR symbol from 2 % up (at 2 %, 7 of 32 versions are over a module, so the threshold is 2 % and it is not confined to short symbols); tightening them means tracing the winning grid's perimeter after a read, a follow-up in [rmqr-decoder.md](rmqr-decoder.md). `System.Numerics.Vector2` was not used because on netstandard2.0 it would add a package dependency to a package that advertises none. No reference library returns this for Standard QR, which is why it was worth a public type.

Image builders: one builder per symbology, all deriving from `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>` (self-referential generic, so fluent chains keep the concrete type). The base carries every shared option and the complete raster/SVG output surface; a symbology builder adds only its typed options (ECC/version) and connects its data model through three `private protected` hooks. Two guards keep the surfaces from drifting: the base class makes output-method omissions structurally impossible, and `QrImageBuilderApiParityTest` (reflection over the public surfaces with a documented allowed-difference list) catches asymmetry in what cannot be shared, the symbology-typed static helpers. The rMQR builder extends the same base and the same parity test.

Capacity pricing overflow: Byte mode costs `8 × length` bits, so a data length past `int.MaxValue / 8` wraps negative and reads as a fit. All three selectors price in `long` — including the UTF-8 BOM's `+ 3`, which wraps on its own near `int.MaxValue`. Widening rather than rejecting the length up front is the deliberate choice: a length fast-path placed ahead of the remaining checks answers "does not fit" for what is actually an argument error, and one placed ahead of the Micro QR version check also handed an unvalidated version to the table-indexing error builder. Reachable only with a quarter-gigabyte input, so `CapacityOverflowGuardTest` drives the selectors directly instead of allocating one.

Sizing: every generator exposes exactly one sizing method, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`, with one contract across all three symbologies — `false` means the content does not fit, and argument errors throw. Standard QR and Micro QR carried an `[Obsolete]` throwing `GetRequiredBufferSize` through 1.2.0, kept only because v1.1.1 released it, and lost it in 2.0.0. `SizingSurfaceTest` asserts the absence rather than assuming it, because a throwing convenience is the kind of thing someone re-adds in good faith. The reasoning, including why this is a `Try` overload rather than a dedicated exception type and why undefined enum values are not folded into `false`, is recorded once in [rmqr-encoder.md](rmqr-encoder.md); the other two symbologies follow it rather than restating it.

Exact API names and shapes are finalized per-symbology at implementation time, spec-first, following the API-driven development principle in [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md).

### Data model direction

`QRCodeData` stays Standard-QR-only. New symbologies get their own data types, with rectangular dimensions (width ≠ height) decided once when the first new type is introduced.

Serialization: the `QRR` format is frozen as-is for Standard QR (header + 1-byte size, sizes 21–177, square). New symbologies use a new serialization header carrying symbol type, width, and height. Old readers reject new-format streams cleanly (the existing header/size validation already guarantees this).

**A value the library hands back is a `readonly record struct` with an internal constructor and get-only properties.** `QRCodeCalculatedSize`, `MicroQRCodeCalculatedSize`, `RmQRCodeCalculatedSize` and the three `*DecodeInfo` types all follow it since 2.0.0; Standard QR's sizing result had a public constructor, `init` setters and an `IsValid` property, the other two were plain structs, and the drift was invisible until someone read all three files side by side. The rule is what the type is *for*: it is an `out` parameter of a `Try` method, so there is no half-built instance to hand back in, `init` would let a caller edit an answer the library computed, and `IsValid` duplicated the `bool` the `Try` already returned. Only positional records deconstruct, so declaring these without positional parameters drops deconstruction and keeps everything else — `ToString`, `==` and `IEquatable<T>` — which is what a caller logging a size or comparing two decode results actually uses. `TypeShapeTest` asserts the shape rather than trusting the next type to copy it.

**Being library-built is not a reason to be opaque, and that took two attempts.** The first cut demoted these to plain structs, which also threw away the printer and non-boxing equality: `size.ToString()` became the type name and `Equals` started boxing both operands. What had to go was the public constructor and the `init` setters; the record was never the problem. The same mistake landed on `GradientOptions` in the same change, where dropping the record silently removed `with`. One rule came out of it: when a type's shape is wrong, name the member that is wrong and remove that, rather than reaching for the enclosing kind.

**The three decode results report the same members under the same names**, with two documented exceptions: rMQR has no `MaskPattern`, because ISO/IEC 23941 defines a single data mask, and only Standard QR has `StructuredAppend`, because neither other standard defines it or has a mode indicator for it. Same for sizing, where rMQR is rectangular (`Width`/`Height`) and the square symbologies report one `Size`.

**An option object a caller builds is immutable once built, and stays varyable with `with`.** The generator options are `readonly record struct`s with `init` members; `IconData` is a `sealed record class` with `init`-only members, and `GradientOptions` is a `sealed record class` that copies the arrays it is given and reads them back as `ReadOnlySpan<T>`. They vary with `with`, which is the point: changing one field of an instance a caller did not construct — a preset from configuration, an `IconData` from a factory method — otherwise means retyping every other field and silently taking the defaults for the ones forgotten.

**A member is `init` when it carries no cross-member invariant, and set through a method or the constructor when it does.** `with` assigns one member at a time, so a pair that must agree cannot be exposed that way: `GradientOptions.Colors` and `ColorPositions` have to be the same length, and making them `init` would let a caller build a gradient whose stops no longer match its colours and discover it at draw time. `Direction` has no such pairing and stays `init`; the pair is set together through the constructor, which refuses the mismatch on the spot. `IconData` needs no such carve-out because none of its members validate against another at construction — its sizing rules are checked when the icon is drawn, so every member can be `init`. The rule is what makes the two types differ, not an oversight in either. `GradientOptions` is where this stopped being theoretical: holding a public `SKColor[]` through an `init` property, its generated equality compared the arrays by reference, so two identical gradients were unequal, and `GradientOptions.Default` — one shared instance — could be repainted for the whole process through the array it exposed. **An immutable type has to be rebuildable from what it hands back.** `GradientOptions` first exposed spans and accepted arrays, with "no stops" reading as an empty span and writing as `null`, so recolouring an existing gradient cost a `ToArray()` and a ternary — and a caller who omitted the ternary silently dropped the stops. The constructor takes spans now, empty meaning evenly distributed on both sides, and the round trip is one expression. The rule generalises: when a value type's getter and its constructor disagree about representation, the migration guide is where the disagreement shows up as an unreadable line, and the guide is the wrong place to fix it.

Equality is written by hand over the elements now, and the array is private, which is also what makes the record's shallow copy safe: `Default with { Direction = … }` shares the colours with `Default`, and no member of either instance hands the array out. The guarantee documented is "immutable through the API" rather than "immutable", because `MemoryMarshal` and reflection both reach past it — not a caveat worth putting in front of callers, but the qualifier keeps a later change from treating the array as unreachable. Dropping the record was tried first and rejected — it took `with` away while the three generator options kept it, and the defect was the *public array*, not the record. `IconData` was demoted the same way in the same change and restored for the same reason.

**Styling reaches the data modules, never the finder patterns.** `WithModuleShape(shape, sizePercent)` and its renderer parameters style the data; the finder patterns are drawn as one continuous concentric pattern whatever is asked for, and `WithFinderPatternShape` (on all three builders) is the only way to change how they look. The split is not aesthetic, it is how the two kinds of module are read: a data module is sampled at the centre of its cell, so gaps around it cost nothing, while a finder is located by scanning for its 1:1:3:1:1 run of dark and light, which a gap of one fiftieth of a module already destroys — the dark three-module centre becomes three runs and the ratio is nowhere in the image. Measured: at 98 % module size the symbol was found by neither this library nor ZXing, on every symbology, so what the old behaviour produced was a non-conformant symbol rather than a styled one (ISO/IEC 15415 grades fixed-pattern damage separately from data for the same reason). Alignment patterns need no such protection and get none: they are found from a predicted position by their single dark centre module, and shrinking them to 75 % still decodes at version 40. The full-size square path is left in the merged-run renderer, where the finder is already solid, so the fast path is untouched and only the per-module path pays anything — and it pays less, three rectangles per finder instead of thirty-three module draws.

**Modules stay square at every canvas aspect ratio the builder accepts, so `WithSize(w, h)` fits rather than stretches.** That is the invariant, and it is deliberately narrower than "every canvas produces a readable symbol": what a reader needs is square modules *and* enough pixels per module, and `WithSize` has no lower bound on the second. A canvas can starve the short side without being small (4000x30 is 0.91 px/module and nothing reads it), so the fit removes one failure mode rather than all of them. The symbol is drawn at one uniform module scale, centered, whatever aspect ratio the caller asks for; leftover canvas is padded with `clearColor` when one is set and with the background colour otherwise. Both halves are corrections of the same defect on the square symbologies (rMQR was built this way, except that its explicit-canvas pad was transparent). The stretch dates to the 2019 renderer, which divided the area by columns and rows independently, and to a public API that took width and height separately from its first release; nothing chose it, and nothing tested it, so it survived into 2.0.0 behind a `preserveAspectRatio` flag whose comment said only that the square symbologies "keep the historical fill behavior". What it produced was undetectable rather than merely ugly: module centres stayed correct, so the data was intact and no call threw, while the finder's 1:1:3:1:1 run only survives on one axis once the cells are rectangular. Sweeping several payloads, four stylings and both orientations through this library and ZXing.Net, failures appear from about 1.25:1 and neither reads anything past about 1.8:1; where a given symbol lands in between moves with the payload, with the styling and with which axis is squeezed, and the two decoders disagree by direction (on wide renders this library reads many ZXing does not; on tall ones ZXing reads many this library does not, though that half depends on ZXing being run with AutoRotate). There is no threshold worth quoting, which is the point — `WithSize(900, 450)` returned an image neither of them reads (zxing-cpp, outside that sweep, reads the migration guide's example, though not every payload), and nothing said so. The pad default follows from the same standard: transparent is the wrong thing to hand back by default, because it becomes black bands the moment the image is encoded as JPEG and it costs the opaque-surface optimization; transparent surroundings around an opaque symbol stay available by naming `clearColor`. The pad is painted around the content rather than under it, so a translucent background is not blended twice.

**The low-level renderer fits its area too, so the library has one geometry rule (2026-09-11).** `SymbolRenderer.Render(canvas, area, …)` and the `SKCanvas.Render` extensions draw Standard QR and Micro QR at one uniform module scale centered in the area, with the background over the whole area, which is what rMQR's overload always did. The public `GetFinderPatternRect` and `GetIconRects` fit the same way, because they answer for the area the caller passed to `Render` and would otherwise point beside what was drawn. For a day after the builders stopped stretching, the renderer kept the fill on purpose, as the only way left to pre-distort a symbol for an output device whose dots are not square, and the plan was to give the builders an axis-aware module size first and only then make the renderer fit. Checking that plan found its premise false. Pre-distortion never needed a stretched area: a non-uniform canvas scale over a square area gives the old fill's pixels exactly for plain modules and finders in a solid colour (0 differing pixels across four aspect ratios; styled output, meaning shaped modules or finders, gradients and icons, is drawn in the square and stretched with it, which can differ from what the old fill drew), and a square area passes through the fit unchanged, so the renderer fits and the device case is served by the canvas transform, where a caller who owns the canvas already says such things. The builder-level `WithModulePixelSize(x, y)` waits for a concrete request: the device use case was named in review to justify the fill and has no report behind it, and it would have to be built as a transform over square cells: the renderer fits any non-square area it is handed to a square, and a path that skipped the fit would still get styled modules wrong, since `CircleModuleShape` sizes its dot from the shorter side of the cell and would print squashed, and the rounded shapes take their corner radius from that side and would print uneven corners. The fit is taken from the shorter side rather than through a module scale, and an area already square to within float rounding comes back exactly as given, so a square area draws what it drew before and fitting twice equals fitting once; the renderer relies on that when it hands an already-fitted area to the helpers. The rounding slack is not optional: `SKRect.Create(x, y, s, s)` stores right and bottom as rounded sums, so a square at fractional coordinates is often a float step from square, and shrinking it by that step moved module edges by a pixel. Two float steps per axis is the floor, not a margin: a square whose four edges are each scaled, which is what a canvas scale produces, comes back two steps from square, measured over three million of them against `SKRect.Create`, centre-and-half and `SKMatrix.MapRect` constructions. The cost of that floor is that far from the origin, where a step is a large share of the area, a rectangle that is not square passes as one: at 1e9 a step is 64, so a 400x600 area is stored as 384x576, one and a half steps from square, and is drawn square. Nothing renders correctly there in any case, because the same step quantises every module edge, and no slack can separate the two: the rectangle is closer to square, in steps, than a real scaled square is. The two limits are far apart, measured on a 400 px symbol: a square area stops decoding at a coordinate of 1.68e7 (2^24), where a step reaches 2 and the module edges quantise, while the slack does not accept a 1.5:1 area until 4.38e8 (2^28.7), twenty-six times further out. Inside the range that still decodes, the widest stretch the slack can accept is about 1 % (1.011:1 at a coordinate of 1e7), against the 1.25:1 where reading starts to fail, so the slack cannot cost a read. The precision is lost in the caller's `SKRect` before the renderer sees it, so no signature taking one can recover it; a caller working at such coordinates keeps the area near the origin and places it with the canvas transform, which is what the rasteriser wants anyway. An inverted area (a negative width or height) is refused with `ArgumentException` in all three symbologies, and so is a non-finite one: an inverted rect reads two ways, a mirror or the same bounds written backwards, and for an asymmetric symbol those are different pictures, so neither is guessed. A mirrored symbol is asked for with a canvas scale of -1 about the area, the same principle as pre-distortion, and the decoder reads mirrored captures, so strict output and tolerant input stay the pair. A zero-size area draws nothing rather than throwing, because a canvas before layout or a collapsed panel produces one routinely; the test is the fitted symbol, so anything sized in pixels rather than in cells (an icon border, a caption, a caller-written shape) stops there too, while invalid icon settings are still refused, since a collapsed panel must not hide a mistake until it opens. An area whose fitted symbol has no size keeps its background, since the area is the caller's and only the symbol is missing; an aspect ratio past about 2^25 reaches that state without being zero, because centring the symbol puts its offset where its shorter side rounds away (rMQR's rectangle survives about three powers of two longer than the square symbologies'). The canvas extensions check every argument before they clear the canvas, so a refused call leaves it as it was, which means the gradient direction is checked up front as well, not left to the draw call that consumes it. What still differs from the builders is rounding: they floor the centering offset to whole pixels because they own the canvas, while the renderer uses the fit as computed because its area may sit under the caller's transform, so an odd leftover can shift edges by half a pixel. The decode side keeps its non-square tolerance: symbols arrive from thermal printers, laser markers and perspective, so an encoder that never produces non-square modules and a decoder that accepts them is the pair that makes sense. The tolerance has a measured edge, the same for all three symbologies and both directions (plain modules 8 px on the short side, three payloads of different versions per symbology, every right-angle rotation, 2026-09-27): every render decodes to 2.35:1, at 2.40:1 only the largest Standard QR payload does, and from 2.45:1 none. The edge is the finder cross-check's: a finder's column may be at most 12/5 as long as its row, a window sized for keystoned finders, and with it widened to 4 the same renders decode to 3.5:1. Before that window (2026-09-26) the column had to be within 40 % of the row, and the edge measured 2026-09-12 was about 1.38:1. With the builders and the renderer fitting every area, a canvas scale is the only way left to make such a symbol, so the decoder tests draw theirs that way and measure the finder's centre stone on both axes to prove the stretch is in the pixels; the tests they replaced had been drawing square modules since the canvas fit, and nothing noticed.

**A public class with no designed extension point is sealed:** the three data types, the three image builders, `IconData` and `GradientOptions`. The extension points are the shape hierarchies (`ModuleShape`, `FinderPatternShape`, `IconShape`), and `SymbolImageBuilderBase<TSelf>`, whose `private protected` constructor keeps derivation inside the rendering package.

## Why

### Why three packages under a new name

Issue #370 named the two strengths of the 1.x library, SkiaSharp integration and speed with low memory, and the contradiction between them: anyone who wanted only the QR module matrices still paid for SkiaSharp. The cost was never the managed assembly (95 KB trimmed to QR encode only); it is `libSkiaSharp`, 11.9 MB per RID, untrimmable, deployed whether or not a Skia call survives, and the part that needs CVE tracking. A dependency graph is fixed only by a package boundary, so the 2.0.0 major split the one package into a dependency-free core and a rendering package (the core split, 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-06).

**The core is not `SkiaSharp.QrCode.Core`.** A dependency-free package must not carry the name of the dependency it is free of; the name would lie to exactly the audience the split is for, and it fails at the second non-Skia renderer (`SkiaSharp.QrCode.ImageSharp` is nonsense). The `SkiaSharp.*` prefix is reserved on nuget.org but public, so the ID was pushable; it was rejected on meaning, not mechanics. The brand became `FeatherQR`: "Feather" is the established .NET word for lightweight (`FeatherHttp`, `Feather.Blazor`, `DotFeather`), lightweight is the title of the issue, and the compound was free on nuget.org, npm, crates.io, PyPI and GitHub. Every speed word considered instead was a benchmark claim, a live product, a reduced-feature connotation, a language, a fictional symbology next to Micro QR, or a .NET-only term. What the name is allowed to mean is defined under "Package architecture" so it never has to be defended against a byte count.

**`SkiaSharp.QrCode` survives as an empty metapackage because NuGet has no redirect.** The three mechanisms that exist are keeping an ID, deprecating it with an alternate (one-way, for retiring), and a metapackage.
